newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. urges China to seize chance for cooperation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges China to seize chance for cooperation.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday praised China for taking steps to improve civil rights and implored Beijing to seize an historic opportunity to build a new era of cooperation.

In a speech at Fudan University outlining a strategic basis for Sino-American ties in the 21st century, he solidified an evolution in the U.S. approach from confrontation to determined dialogue and joint action on a broad range of issues.

Profound differences -- including over human rights and Taiwan -- must not be allowed to "undermine our ability to achieve common goals", Christopher told an audience of students, faculty and local Chinese officials.

"Now more than ever before, the American and Chinese people can and must work together to advance our interests," he said. "Like all great nations, we will no doubt at times have divergent views. But history has given our two countries a remarkable opportunity -- the opportunity to build a new era of cooperation for a new century. It is an opportunity we simply must seize," Christopher said.
"As nuclear powers, permanent members of the U.N. Security Council and two of the world's biggest economies, we must lead" to promote global peace and prosperity, he added.

His spokesman called the speech a turning point. "This is the first time we are saying publicly that the future of the relationship is not adversarial, not rivalry...it's partnership," Nicholas Burns told reporters.

However, while use of the word partnership to describe U.S.- China ties was discussed by U.S. officials, it was ultimately left out of the speech because they decided the still fragile relationship had not reached that point.
Christopher flew to Shanghai for a one-day stop after talks on Wednesday with senior Chinese officials in Beijing intended to ensure shaky Sino-American ties are back on track.
The trip marked the highest-level visit to the Chinese capital by a senior U.S. official since Christopher's last trip in 1994, a disaster because of rows over human rights.
Later, he toured Shanghai, where as a lawyer in the 1980s he represented U.S. firms now fuelling the economic boom in China's financial capital.
In the speech, Christopher acknowledged continuing disputes between communist China and Washington over human rights.
But despite Beijing's recent new severe crackdown on dissidents -- which the secretary did not mentioned publicly in explicit terms -- Christopher found progress on civil rights.

"China's recent efforts to invest authority in its people through legal and administrative reforms and village elections are a positive step in that direction" towards the rule of law, he said, referring to recent reforms of criminal procedures and efforts to develop a commercial code.

In another sign of a new U.S. deference on human rights, Christopher told a student who questioned him after the speech that "each nation with its own history and own set of requirements must find its own way on this subject".

Although he also stressed the need to recognise "the dignity of the individual and the need to treat the individual with concern and care and compassion", the overall tone of his public remarks on this subject was a far cry from 1992.

Then, during his first campaign for the White House, Bill Clinton argued that favourable trade benefits should be tied to China's human rights record and scored then President George Bush for "coddling communist dictators" in Beijing.
Two years later, Clinton dropped the link between trade and rights and recently has moved with increasing speed to cooperate with China despite continued repression in Beijing.

U.S. officials, including Christopher, say China's record remains a great concern. But they argue progress on other fronts -- including trade and global security issues -- cannot be hostage to this one topic.

Washington has been touting a new "engagement" with China but Christopher dropped that term from his speech because China experts say its translates in Chinese as "contact" and hence has not reassured China as the Americans hoped it would.
Christopher acknowledged this fact publicly on Thursday, drawing sympathetic laughter from his audience and applause when he said what Washington means is "intensive dialogue".
